Hello everyone! My name is Komugill, and I study in 8th standard at Hindusthan School.

My favourite subject is Maths. I enjoy solving problems and finding the answer step by step, and it makes me feel proud when I get a tough question right.

Outside of studies, I love playing cricket. It keeps me active and teaches me teamwork, patience, and how to stay calm under pressure.

Interestingly, cricket and Maths are connected. Batting averages, strike rates, and run rates are all Maths in action!
summary:
Overview

Relics is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of the equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. Instead of treating these objects as space junk, it presents each one as a character in humanity’s exploration story, with a purpose, an achievement, an ending and a lesson. Visitors choose a world, tap a relic on a map, and read what the object did, why it was left, what condition it is in, and what we learned from it.

The Problem

Most people know that astronauts walked on the Moon and that rovers have driven across Mars, but very few know what remains there today. Descent stages, lunar rovers, landers, instruments and even a helicopter still sit where their missions ended. Information about them is spread across technical archives, mission pages and image libraries that are difficult for students and the general public to navigate.
The topic is also becoming more relevant. NASA’s Artemis program is preparing to return people to the Moon, and commercial missions are following. That raises practical questions: how should historic landing sites be protected, and what can aged hardware teach us about building equipment that lasts? These questions deserve public attention, and storytelling is one of the best ways to create it.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Relics is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. A visitor chooses a world, then explores a coordinate map where each pin marks a relic’s approximate landing location. A date-ordered list sits beside the map, so any story can be reached either way.

Selecting a relic opens a story card with four parts:

  • Current state: where the object is now and what condition it is in
  • Its story: what it was built to do and why it was left behind
  • What we learned: the lesson it offers future missions
  • NASA images: a link to NASA’s image library, so visitors can see real photographs

The prototype covers twelve relics. On the Moon these are the Apollo 11 descent stage, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 12 visit, and the lunar rovers from Apollo 15, 16 and 17. On Mars they are the Viking 1 and 2 landers, Sojourner and Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. A short quiz at the end reinforces what visitors learned.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns scattered technical records into short, readable stories for students, teachers and the general public.
  • It needs no installation or account, loads quickly, and works on phones and computers.
  • It is accessible, with keyboard navigation, visible focus states, light and dark themes, and reduced-motion support.
  • The quiz and the consistent story format make it useful in classrooms.
  • New relics are easy to add, because every entry follows the same data structure.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to see these machines as part of a shared human journey rather than as space junk. As NASA’s Artemis program returns people to the Moon, we hope the project builds public awareness of why preserving historic landing sites matters, and of what aged hardware can teach us about building equipment that lasts in dust, vacuum and radiation. It also aims to inspire curiosity in younger audiences about planetary exploration.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Format: a single self-contained web page with no external libraries
  • Data: a structured data set listing each relic’s name, site, coordinates, year, status, story and lesson
  • Hosting: a public web link, so no installation is needed
  • Presentation: a 7-slide demo deck
  • AI assistance: an AI assistant (Claude) helped draft the story text, summary and page code
  • Hardware: any ordinary computer or phone; the project needs nothing special
  • Reference sources: NASA Image and Video Library, NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek, LROC (Arizona State University), HiRISE (University of Arizona), and NASA mission pages

How is the project creative?

  • Objects as characters: Each relic is written as a character with a purpose, an achievement, an ending and a lesson, not as a catalog entry.
  • Human-scale details: Opportunity was built for months and lasted nearly fifteen years. Apollo 12 astronauts walked to Surveyor 3 and brought parts home. These details make the history memorable.
  • Museum-placard design: The page uses calm typography and a structure like a museum placard, so the relics feel like heritage rather than debris.
  • Two worlds, one map style: The Moon and Mars share one interface, which invites visitors to compare how exploration differs between them.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: Mission facts and coordinates must be verified against NASA sources. All locations on the map are approximate.
  • Clear creative framing: Stories are plain retellings, and any creative narration should be labeled as interpretation, not NASA quotes.
  • Honest AI use: We disclose that an AI assistant helped with drafting and code, and that a human team reviews the content.
  • Licensing: NASA imagery is linked rather than copied, and any future use should credit NASA, ASU and the University of Arizona.
  • Accessibility and reach: The design supports many devices and abilities, and future versions could add narration and more languages.
  • Scope: We kept the first version focused on twelve well-documented relics, rather than a large catalog done poorly.
  • Heritage and ethics: The project respects the historic value of the sites and does not claim NASA endorsement.

Before submitting, check the facts and coordinates against NASA sources and edit any statement that doesn’t match what your team actually did.
